title: Tyagaraja
wiki_lead:
Sadguru Sri Tyāgarāja Swāmi (4 May 1767 – 6 January 1847), also known as Tyāgayya, and in full as Kākarla Tyāgabraḥmaṁ, was a composer of Carnatic Music, a form of Indian Classical Music. Tyāgarāja and his contemporaries, Śyāma Śāstri and Muthuswāmi Dikshitar, are regarded as the Trinity of Carnatic Music. Tyāgarāja composed hundreds of devotional kṛti (transl. compositions), mostly in Telugu and in praise of Rāma. Many of them remain popular to this day. Of special mention are five of his compositions called the Pañcaratna Kṛti (transl. five gems), which are often sung in programs held in his honor. Tyāgarāja composed many Utsava Sāmpradāya Kṛti (transl. festive ritual compositions), meant to be sung in temple rituals/festivities and Divya Nāma Saṅkīrtana (transl. divine compositions on the Lord's various names), sung as a part of concerts and daily life.
Tyāgarāja lived through the reigns of four kings of the Thanjavur Maratha rule – Thuljaji (1763–1787), Amarasimha (1787–1798), Serfoji II (1798–1832) and Shivaji II (1832–1855), although he served none of them.

Tyāgarāja and his contemporaries, Śyāma Śāstri and Muthuswāmi Dikshitar, are regarded as the Trinity of Carnatic Music. Tyāgarāja composed hundreds of devotional kṛti (transl. compositions), mostly in Telugu and in praise of Rāma. Many of them remain popular to this day. Of special mention are five of his compositions called the Pañcaratna Kṛti (transl. five gems), which are often sung in programs held in his honor. Tyāgarāja composed many Utsava Sāmpradāya Kṛti (transl. festive ritual compositions), meant to be sung in temple rituals/festivities and Divya Nāma Saṅkīrtana (transl. divine compositions on the Lord's various names), sung as a part of concerts and daily life.
Tyāgarāja lived through the reigns of four kings of the Thanjavur Maratha rule – Thuljaji (1763–1787), Amarasimha (1787–1798), Serfoji II (1798–1832) and Shivaji II (1832–1855), although he served none of them.


Biography
Tyāgarāja was born Kākarla Tyāgabraḥmaṁ in 1767 to a Telugu Vaidiki Mulakanādu Brahmin family in Thiruvarur, present-day Thiruvarur District of Tamil Nadu. There is a school of thought led by the musicologist B.M.Sundaram that contests this and proposes Thiruvaiyaru, in Thanjavur District of Tamil Nadu, as his birth place,  though there is little evidence for this. His family name Kākarla indicates that his family had their roots in the village of the same name in Kambham, Mārkapuraṁ division of Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh (called the Kurnool region of Prakasam district) and migrated to present-day Tamil Nadu after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire. His family belonged to the Smārta tradition and Bharadwāja gotra. Tyāgarāja was the third son of his parents, Kākarla Rāmabraḥmaṁ and Sītamma.
Tyāgarāja's paternal grandfather was Kākarla Girirāja Braḥmaṁ/Girirāja Kavi (not the name-sake Giriraja Kavi).

Girirāja Braḥmaṁ was a poet, scholar and a musician. He was born in Kākarla village, Kambham mandal, Mārkapuraṁ division of Prakasam District, in present-day Andhra Pradesh. Tyāgarāja's maternal grandfather was Kāḷahastayya, popularly addressed as Vīṇa Kāḷahastayya as he was a noted Vīṇa player. Tyāgarāja was said to have learnt to play the vīṇa in his childhood from Kāḷahastayya. After Kāḷahastayya's death, Tyāgarāja was said to have found Nāradīyam, a book on music.
Tyāgarāja was married to Parvati and after her death, he subsequently married her sister, Kamala.
Tyāgarāja spent most of his life in Thiruvaiyaru in the single room house (No. 31, Thirumanjana Veedhi) that was donated to his father Rāmabraḥmaṁ by Thuljaji, in whose court Rāmabraḥmaṁ worked. This house has since been renovated and opened to music lovers after years of neglect. There are records of his pilgrimage to Sri Raṅgaṁ, Tirumala and Kāñcipuraṁ. On his Kāñcipuraṁ pilgirmage, records mention him meeting the seer Upanishad Brahmayogin at the Braḥmendraḷ Maṭha
Tyāgarāja took siddhi (transl. attained liberation) on Puṣya Bahuḷa Pañcami - 6 January 1847, at the age of 79, a day after he took the vow of sanyāsa and was initiated into the order of Advāita Daśanāmi Saṁpradāya of sainthood. His last composition was Giripai Nelakonna (గిరిపై నెలకొన్న) in Rāga Sahānā, set to Ādi Tāḷa. He was interred on the banks of the river Kāveri river at Thiruvaiyaru the very next day.


Musical career

Tyagaraja began his musical training at an early age under Sonthi Venkata Ramanayya, the chief vidwan in the court of Thanjavur ruler Thuljaji, where Tyagaraja's father Ramabrahmam also worked. Tyagaraja hero-worshipped the celestial sage Narada; a reference to this is Tyagaraja's krithi Vara Nārada (rāga Vijayaśrī, Ādi tāḷam). grok_lead: Tyagaraja (1767â1847), also known as Tyagabrahmam or Saint Tyagaraja, was a revered composer, singer, and poet in the Carnatic classical music tradition of South India, celebrated for his thousands of devotional compositions called kritis, most of which extol the virtues of the Hindu god Rama. Born into a Telugu Brahmin family in Tiruvarur, Tamil Nadu, he exemplified a life of bhakti (devotion) and musical innovation, contributing profoundly to the evolution of Carnatic music through his lyrical depth, melodic explorations, and emphasis on spiritual themes. As one of the Carnatic music trinity alongside Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri, Tyagaraja's works, said to have aimed at 24,000 compositions mirroring Valmiki's Ramayana with around 700 surviving today, remain central to concert repertoires and embody a synthesis of music, poetry, and philosophy rooted in Hindu scriptures. Tyagaraja was born on May 4, 1767, in Tiruvarur to Rama Brahmam, a musician proficient in veena and vocals, and Sitamma, within a family of scholars and artists influenced by the Tanjore court. From an early age, he displayed prodigious talent, receiving formal training in music from Sonti Venkataramanayya and literary education in Telugu, Sanskrit, Vedas, and poetics from his father Ramabrahmam, which shaped his versatile command over kavya (poetry), alankara (rhetoric), and nataka (drama). He married twiceâfirst to Parvati, who died young, and then to Kanakambaâand lived modestly through alms (unchavritti), rejecting invitations for royal patronage, such as from the Tanjore ruler, to pursue his ascetic devotion. His travels included pilgrimages to Tirupati, Madras, and Kanchipuram in 1839, where he composed and performed, fostering disciples who disseminated his teachings across South India. The core of Tyagaraja's oeuvre consists of kritis in Telugu, with some in Sanskrit, structured in a tripartite formâpallavi ( refrain), anupallavi (sub-refrain), and charanam ( stanza)âand enriched by sangatis, melodic variations that he popularized to enhance expressiveness and rhythmic interplay. He employed over 250 ragas (melodic frameworks) and aimed to create 24,000 songs mirroring Valmiki's Ramayana, infusing them with philosophical insights from the Upanishads, Puranas, and bhakti traditions, as seen in works like "Prahlada Bhakti Vijayam" (a five-act opera with 45 kritis) and "Nauka Charitam" (a one-act play). Notable examples include the Pancharatna Kritisâ"JagadanandakÄraka" in NÄta rÄga and "Dudukugala" in ChÄyÄnÄá¹­aâwhich highlight his mastery in blending devotion, emotion, and technical precision. Tyagaraja passed away on January 6, 1847, in Tiruvaiyaru, where his samadhi (memorial) now hosts the annual Tyagaraja Aradhana festival on Pushya Bahula Panchami, drawing thousands for communal singing of his compositions. His legacy endures as the cornerstone of modern Carnatic music, elevating Telugu as a medium for divine poetry and establishing kritis as the genre's dominant form by the late 19th century, influencing generations of musicians and devotees. Through nadopasana (worship via music), Tyagaraja transformed Carnatic music into a vehicle for spiritual realization, ensuring its vitality in contemporary performances and cultural practices.
